entries.title: Introducing Search for Agents
entries.summary: Flip one toggle to make your site searchable by AI agents — complete with automatic content indexing, a discoverable search API, and native HTTP QUERY support.
entries.content:
AI Search, our service that indexes your content and lets you add search to any application or agent without having to build an entire retrieval infrastructure, has supported adding your website as a data source for a while now, automatically crawling, converting and indexing its pages.

Still, setting up an AI Search instance for your website requires manually creating and configuring it initially, and then doing all the integration work to get the search endpoints available from your domain and to make sure that agents know where to find the index and know how to use it.

Today we're introducing Search for Agents, which puts that setup behind a toggle in your Cloudflare dashboard. Turn it on for your zone, and our service will create your AI Search instance, start indexing your content, and make search discoverable and available from your own domain.

How it works

The idea follows naturally from Markdown for Agents, where Cloudflare's network converts any HTML page to Markdown in real time for enabled zones using content negotiation headers. Similarly, Search for Agents leverages the power of AI Search by automatically creating an index for your zone and exposing APIs that any AI agent can discover and use to search your website, under your domain, all done at the network level.

You can enable Search for Agents using the API, or by going to the dashboard in your zone page, under Quick Actions:

Search for Agents is available to all customers, including Free (with limits). Once it’s enabled, Cloudflare will automatically create an AI Search instance, start crawling and indexing the content in your zone. Refer to our developer documentation  to understand how the crawling process works.

You can access your instance directly from this page, or by going to directly to your account’s AI > AI Search instances view:

The AI Search instance for your zone is created with default settings, but you can enable reranking or change configuration options like cache settings at any time. Refer to our documentation for the full list of options.

Once AI Search indexes your content, you or any agent on the Internet can start using Search for Agents, subject to your domain settings (e.g. your bot management settings, AI Crawl Control and web application firewall (WAF) configurations).

Discoverability

Search isn't much use if the agents don’t know it's there. To facilitate discoverability, Search for Agents automatically advertises the search endpoint on every page of your site.

For example, for HTML responses, we add metadata to the page's :

      
<meta
<meta
<meta
<meta

If you also have Markdown for Agents enabled, an agent requesting a page with Accept: text/markdown receives the same information in YAML front matter:

      
---
agent:
  instructions: "Use this search API to find relevant content across this site with keywords or natural-language queries, instead of crawling individual pages. Results are returned in Markdown."
  endpoint: "https://developers.cloudflare.com/.well-known/search?q={query}"
  method: "GET"
  documentation: "https://developers.cloudflare.com/ai-search/how-to/search-for-agents/"
---

The agent will easily pick up these instructions and know what to do next to search your site.

Searching content

Once the agent knows that your site has a search endpoint, it can start using it:

      
$ curl "https://developers.cloudflare.com/.well-known/search?q=cloudflare+artifacts"
# Search results for: "cloudflare artifacts"

## docs/artifacts/api/workers-binding/index.md (score: 1.000)

# Workers binding · Artifacts · Cloudflare Artifacts docs

Call Artifacts from a Worker binding.

---

## docs/artifacts/index.md (score: 0.951)

# Artifacts · Cloudflare Artifacts docs

Store, version, and share filesystem artifacts across Workers, APIs, and Git-compatible tools.
...

Depending on your AI Search configuration, the agent can also use natural language and ask questions to the search endpoint:

      
$ curl --get "https://developers.cloudflare.com/.well-known/search" --data-urlencode "q=What is the maximum push size for Cloudflare Artifacts?"
# Search results for: "What is the maximum push size for Cloudflare Artifacts?"

## docs/artifacts/platform/limits/index.limits-cloudflare-artifacts-docs.md (score: 1.000)

# Limits · Cloudflare Artifacts docs
Section: Limits · Cloudflare Artifacts docs

title: Limits
description: Review Artifacts platform limits.
pcx_content_type: reference
products:
  - artifacts

Limits that apply to creating, importing, cloning, and pushing Artifacts are detailed below.

These limits cover naming rules, storage, request rates for control-plane and Git operations, and the size of each push.

FeatureLimitControl-plane request rate2,000 requests per 10 seconds per Artifacts namespaceGit request rate, per artifact2,000 requests per 10 seconds per artifactMaximum storage per repository1 GB for repos created on or after 2026-09-29. Repos created earlier have a 10 GB limit. See size limit change.Maximum storage per account1 TB (can be raised on request)Maximum number of repositoriesUnlimitedMaximum number of namespacesUnlimitedNamespace name length2–63 charactersNamespace and repo namesStart with a letter or digit. Remaining characters may include letters, digits, ., _, and -.Maximum push size64 MiB per push. Includes all data sent in the push. Split larger work into several smaller pushes.Maximum objects per push50,000 objects, such as file versions, folders, and commits.Maximum file size32 MiB per file. Already-compressed files, like images, video, or zip archives, may be rejected slightly below 32 MiB.Maximum ref updates per push1 MiB of branch and tag updates per push.Maximum entries per folder100,000 files and subfolders in a single folder.
...

Note that this search endpoint returns retrieved content, in Markdown, not a generated answer. The agent already has an AI model and a conversation with the user; all it needs is the relevant information from your site, not another AI model's attempt to answer on its behalf.

Supporting a new HTTP method: QUERY

The new HTTP QUERY method is an IETF Proposed Standard, incidentally coauthored by our own James Snell, published in June 2026 as RFC 10008. A QUERY allows a client to send search criteria in a request body safely and idempotently without modifying server state. This makes it a good fit for AI search.

The adoption of QUERY is underway with major browser vendors discussing the RFC and multiple frameworks and clients either adopting (curl and undici, for example), or discussing adoption.

Search for Agents supports QUERY natively either using a plain text or JSON request body:

      
# Plain text
curl -X QUERY 'https://developers.cloudflare.com/.well-known/search' \
  --data 'What is the maximum payload size per ingestion request in Basin Pipelines?'

# JSON
curl -X QUERY 'https://developers.cloudflare.com/.well-known/search' \
  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"q":"How many bulk import requests per minute does Email Service allow?"}'

See it in action

Let’s see it in action during an agentic session. Search for Agents is enabled for our Developer Documentation. When we open an OpenCode session and ask “What is the maximum push size for Cloudflare Artifacts?”, in the logs we can see the agent discovering the search endpoint on the homepage and then fetching /.well-known/search with the question for the search results.

The answer comes back a few seconds later and it’s correct.

Once the agent discovers the search API, it will likely reuse it multiple times within the same session whenever it needs to search for content in the same site.

We enabled Search for Agents for our developer documentation ahead of this announcement and we’ve found that agents do a good job of discovering the search API and using it during their tasks.

It’s still an AI Search instance

Because Search for Agents is powered by an AI Search instance in your account, you get all the standard configuration options and features as well. For example, you can enable public REST API or MCP endpoints, or use it from Workers, or even embed AI Search on your website for human visitors.

Start using Search for Agents

Starting today, Search for Agents is available to all customers. The usage follows the AI Search pricing; that includes ingesting content, storing the index's content, and serving queries, subject to the account's included usage and limits for both the Workers Free and Paid plans.

We also recommend you check our Agent Readiness page (see announcement) and understand how you can make your sites optimized for agents, from guiding agents on how to authenticate, to controlling what content agents can see, the format they receive it in, and how they pay for it.

Check out the Search for Agents developer docs for more information. Follow us on X or come and talk to us in the Cloudflare Developer Discord. We'd like to hear from site owners making their content searchable to agents.

entries.title: Probing DNS at Cloudflare
entries.summary: At Cloudflare we’ve built tools to enable teams to extend our internal testing framework and build test tooling for networking protocols. This is the story of how this was used for DNS.
entries.content:
Imagine this: you’ve just pushed a release. All the unit tests passed and your dashboards are green. You sit back to relax but then suddenly your phone starts blowing up: prod is broken.

This is something the Cloudflare DNS team has experienced firsthand. In one rollout of the service that publishes DNS records to our edge, a scheduling bug let some record changes sit unpublished for hours. The service stayed up and was healthy, but new hostnames were slow to resolve and certificates couldn't be issued until the bug was squashed.

DNS failures are hard to catch because they are slow, spread across the network, and partial in where they cause impact. We needed to figure out a way to test DNS the way customers experience it: constantly, from every data center, and against production.

For us, the answer was to extend Flamingo, the end-to-end testing framework we were already using to run hundreds of millions of tests a day against Cloudflare's edge. This post covers how Flamingo's modular design lets us add DNS support, how we measure propagation, and how those measurements now decide whether a release goes ahead or gets rolled back.

A little background

At Cloudflare we’re obsessed with improving performance and safety for our customers. It’s crucial that our code is tested constantly, both at scale and against the real Cloudflare edge that our users operate in. That’s one reason why we created a tool called Flamingo: to measure the behavior of our production environments and make sure that code in lower-tier environments behaves as expected.

We’ve already written a little about how this tool has been used in the upgrades to our CDN stack. However, this is only a small portion of how we use Flamingo internally. One of the features of Flamingo is its modular architecture that enables teams to extend the capabilities of the tool to speak other networking protocols. In our case, we wanted to use these modular capabilities to test DNS.

What is Flamingo?

Testing is hard. Testing at scale, when you have a widely distributed system, is even harder. There are many complex pathways that requests take and multiple systems that each network request must traverse before making its way to the origin. Unit testing alone is not nearly enough for this. We need to run constant automated testing against real systems and measure the outcomes of those requests to make informed decisions on the health of a service.

Enter Flamingo. Originally built around complex multi-step HTTP testing, its capabilities and scope have increased substantially over the years. Flamingo is built from the ground up with Cloudflare’s infrastructure in mind. We built a control plane and scheduler that let teams target specific environments, data centers, or percentages of metals. We needed to integrate with custom reporting, metrics, and analytics tooling. Additionally, it needed to be a tool with predictable performance and run well on bare-metal servers in resource-constrained environments.

Being delightful

When we’re building internal tooling like this, we strive to create a delightful developer experience. Internal tooling should be as easy as possible to use, but also powerful enough to handle over 80% of all use cases. And in order for a new edge acceptance test framework to be successful, it needs to be built in such a way that it forces teams to follow common guidelines and build reusable scripts in an environment that is stable, scalable, and manages complexity.

One thing that is not delightful is debugging a test. If you allow a user to write tests in a traditional programming language, when their test fails they then both need to debug the upstream system being tested and the test itself. This is why we built Flamingo to use a custom domain-specific language (DSL) consisting of a simple setup-request-response format.

For example, let’s imagine that we want to make sure we are redirecting all unencrypted traffic to its encrypted counterpart.

      
TEST test-redirect
SET $hostname www.cloudflare.com

GET "http://$(hostname)/"

ASSERT STATUS IS 301
ASSERT HEADER Location IS "https://$(hostname)/"

Here we can see the power of the DSL. In five lines of code, we have a script that can run anywhere on Cloudflare’s edge and scale to thousands of requests per minute. We can take the data produced from the millions of data points generated from this and turn those into a graph defining how our service is actually performing in the real world.

Taking the setup-request-response test format from above and modifying it slightly allows us to use Flamingo for more than just HTTP testing. Instead of the middle step being a request, we can now look at it as an action. Now we’ve changed our system from something that makes HTTP requests into something that can perform any action for which we’d like to measure the outcome.

In Flamingo we call these modules and have put immense effort into making them as easy as possible for anyone to write. Flamingo is written in Rust, due to its consistent performance characteristics and strong type system. The type system in particular lends itself to this modularity, by allowing us to use strongly-typed enumerations for input and output in the Flamingo action runner:

      
pub enum Action {
  Query {
    method: String,
    url: Expression,
    parameters: Vec,
  },
  DnsQuery {
    query_name: Expression,
    query_type: Expression,
    parameters: Vec,
  },
}

pub enum ActionOutput {
  Http(http::FetchResponse),
  Dns(dns::QueryResponse),
}

pub type ActionHandlerFunction = Arc<
  dyn Fn(
      Action,
      Arc,
      InterpreterConfig,
    )
      -> BoxFuture<'static, Result>
    + Send
    + Sync
    + 'static,
>;

pub type ActionHandlerLUT = Arc<
  dyn Fn(&Action) -> ActionHandlerFunction
    + Send
    + Sync
    + 'static,
>;

What we’ve done here is decouple the logic for performing an action (in this case an HTTP request) into a dynamically dispatched function that we can then call independently of other actions. This leaves things like test scheduling and resource management as higher-level operations that someone implementing a module doesn’t need to worry about. All the author needs to focus on is the logic.

      
pub async fn query(
  action: Action,
  ctx: Arc,
  cfg: InterpreterConfig,
) -> Result {
  let Action::Query {
    method,
    url,
    parameters,
  } = action
  else {
    bail!("Invalid action for module-http::query: {action:?}");
  };
  ...
}

pub async fn execute_module(
  ctx: Arc,
  cfg: &InterpreterConfig,
  handler_lut: F,
) -> Result
where
  F: (Fn(&Action) -> ActionHandlerFunction),
{
  let func = handler_lut(action);
  let action_out = (func)(action.clone(), ctx.clone(), cfg.clone()).await?;
  ...
}

Using Flamingo to probe DNS

The adage says that when issues arise, it's always DNS. Like many jokes, there is always a kernel of truth behind it. DNS is an incredibly important piece of the Internet, and since it relies on a complex network of interconnected sources of truth, it can become easy for a single misstep to cause a storm of failures.

DNS can be a particularly finicky system due to its hierarchical nature. When you change a DNS record for a Cloudflare zone, for example, said record needs to be propagated to the authoritative servers such that the updated record becomes widely available. To reduce latency, records are stored in physically closer caches. These records have a time to live (TTL) associated with them that tells the local DNS cache how long before it needs to refetch that record from the authoritative server. Any delays will impact time-sensitive operations like certificate issuance and traffic failover.

We’ve already mentioned that we built Flamingo for extensibility. One of the first and most impactful modules in use today was built specifically for this use case. Our team was able to add code that extended Flamingo such that instead of sending HTTP requests, we send DNS queries. By doing so we got everything else for free. No need for the DNS team to worry about managing a new probing service. No need for them to have to integrate with our reporting pipelines. It all just worked.

To probe DNS, we measure how quickly customer record changes propagate to authoritative nameservers and the public resolver (1.1.1.1). The test continuously updates a TXT record with a timestamp and queries three authoritative nameserver IPs and 1.1.1.1 from every data center, asserting freshness within 90s (authoritative) and 600s (resolver).

      
TEST test-propagation-delay-direct-108-162-193-62
MOD dns

SET $hostname "some.probe.domain"
SET $authNs 108.162.193.62:53 # amir.ns.cloudflare.com

QUERY $hostname TXT
TARGET $authNs

ASSERT DNS.RCODE IS NOERROR
ASSERT DNS.FLAGS CONTAINS AA
ASSERT DNS.ANSWERS[0] GT SUBTRACT(TIMESTAMP(), "90")

Catching bugs (SLO and steady)

To ensure that our many systems are operating within expectations, we define what are called service-level objectives (SLOs) for observing things like availability or latency. SLOs are a percentage of some metric that is used as a target. Additionally, SLOs are measured through service-level indicators (SLIs) which are the actual series of measurements focused on the end-to-end experience that a user has when interacting with a system.

By constantly sending synthetic Flamingo traffic through our production systems, we can begin to then use that information to build a picture of what our actual end users are experiencing — and provide that data for our SLOs. When that synthetic traffic encounters issues then we can be pretty confident that Cloudflare customers are also hitting issues and triage accordingly.

Once we have this information, it allows us to make informed decisions when releasing a service. SLOs operate in terms of error budgets and burn rates. An error budget is the percentage of downtime that a service is willing to tolerate while the burn rate is the rate of change in that budget at any given time. This allows for an automated system to understand the severity of an issue. For example, burning 10% of your error budget over a three-day period might be some long running issue that, while not urgent, is affecting customers and needs to be dealt with. But if you were to burn 10% of your error budget within an hour, that means an incident is occurring and customer impact will be substantial if not fixed immediately.

Using these numbers, we can look at our SLOs while deploying and make informed decisions on the health of a service. Based on that information, we can tell our releasing systems to either promote a change or roll it back.

The road ahead

By moving DNS monitoring to Flamingo, we’ve created a system that can proactively detect DNS issues before they have the chance to spread to the rest of Cloudflare’s edge. If Flamingo detects a spike in propagation latency in a specific canary data center, we can automatically halt the rollout of a new software version before it impacts the rest of the Internet.

DNS is just the start for extending Flamingo. We currently have modules for testing TCP, UDP, WebSockets, and several more. Having a tool for quickly testing and monitoring services has enabled teams to deploy large changes safely without the need for a human to keep a constant watch.

If this kind of reliability engineering interests you, check out our careers page for open roles.

entries.title: How Cloudflare WAF protects against ruby2shell (CVE-2026-132825)
entries.summary: ruby2shell lets attackers corrupt memory in default Rails and Sinatra apps without logging in. Cloudflare WAF blocks it for every customer, including Free plans. Upgrade Ruby now, and use the WAF to cover the gap.
entries.content:
On November 19, 2026, the Ruby team disclosed ruby2shell (CVE-2026-132825), a heap buffer overflow in the way Ruby changes the case of strings. Ruby rates the flaw Critical and says it is aware of proofs of concept that achieve remote code execution in some scenarios. Fixes shipped in Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13, and 4.0.10.

The reach is wide. Veria Labs reports that Ruby on Rails and classic-style Sinatra applications reach the bug in their default configuration, before any authentication. Self-hosted products that bundle Ruby, including GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server, Mastodon, OpenProject, Discourse and Chatwoot, shipped an affected Ruby in their latest release at the time of disclosure.

Cloudflare WAF blocks ruby2shell for all customers, including those on the Free plan. We have added two rules to both the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset and the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset, with Block as the default action: one for ruby2shell and one for GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px, a related integer overflow in Ruby string case conversion fixed in the same releases.

The WAF is a compensating control, not a replacement for patching. Exploits can reach the bug through paths a WAF does not see, and the only complete fix is to upgrade Ruby. Our team continues to monitor attack traffic and will update the rules as new techniques appear. You can track rule changes in the WAF changelog and get the latest on the vulnerability in the Cloudflare Zero Wire briefing.

Cloudflare has patched its own systems that use Ruby, and we have found no indication of compromise.

What we know about ruby2shell

Ruby strings carry an encoding, and Ruby still supports many legacy single-byte encodings, such as ISO-8859-1 (Latin-1) and Windows-1252, alongside UTF-8. In a single-byte encoding each character takes one byte, so changing the case of a string usually produces output of the same length.

The German sharp s (ß) breaks that assumption. Its uppercase form is two characters, SS. In 14 ISO-8859 and Windows-125x encodings, Ruby writes those two bytes but checks for room for only one. According to Veria Labs, a string with 21 sharp s characters overflows the output buffer by one byte. The methods that reach the bug are 

upcase
, 
swapcase
, 
downcase(:fold)
 and 
casecmp?
. UTF-8 strings take a different code path and are not affected.

A one-byte overflow can look harmless. In a memory-corruption exploit, though, a single byte written past the end of a heap buffer can be enough to corrupt an adjacent object or allocator metadata. Ruby says it is aware of proofs of concept that turn this flaw into code execution, and Veria Labs says it will publish its own proof of concept about a week after disclosure. We expect scanning to start soon after.

Why default Rails and Sinatra apps are exposed

HTML forms can only send GET and POST requests. To simulate PUT, PATCH, or DELETE, many web frameworks accept a 

_method
 parameter in a POST request. Rack, the interface most Ruby web frameworks build on, implements this in its MethodOverride middleware, which converts the value of 
_method
 to uppercase. Rails includes this middleware by default, and classic-style Sinatra applications enable it. An attacker can send a multipart POST request whose 
_method
 part declares a legacy character set and contains a run of sharp s characters. The framework upcases the value while it is still routing the request, before any application code or authentication check runs.

Veria Labs reports that other frameworks and plain Rack applications are not exposed by default. Application code that changes the case of strings received in a legacy encoding may still be affected, wherever the string comes from.

Who is affected

Condition

Details

Ruby version

Ruby 3.3.13 and earlier, 3.4.0 through 3.4.12, and 4.0.0 through 4.0.9. Veria Labs reports the bug has been present since Ruby 2.4.0. Ruby 3.2 and earlier have reached end of life and will not receive the fix.

Framework

Rails and classic-style Sinatra in their default configuration. Any other code that changes the case of attacker-controlled strings in a legacy single-byte encoding.

Bundled software

As of November 19, 2026, Veria Labs lists GitLab 19.6.0, GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22.5, Mastodon 4.7.5, OpenProject 17.9.7, Discourse 2026.10.1 and Chatwoot 4.20.0 as bundling an affected Ruby in their latest release. Discourse moved its Docker base image to Ruby 4.0.10 on November 19, so rebuilding a Docker install picks up the fix.

Distribution packages can backport fixes without changing the Ruby version number, so check the full package version against your distribution's advisory.

Six more Ruby flaws in the same release

Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13, and 4.0.10 also fix six other memory safety flaws, and Ruby says several of them can lead to code execution. One, GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px, is an integer overflow in the same string case conversion code, and our second WAF rule covers it. The other five are in Ruby's regular expression engine. Most of them require the application to compile or match a regular expression pattern supplied by the attacker. That is uncommon in web applications, but it does happen in search features, filtering rules and admin tools.

How Cloudflare WAF protects you

Upgrading every Ruby runtime takes time, especially when Ruby is bundled inside self-hosted products and container images. Cloudflare WAF reduces your exposure while you patch.

New managed rules, on for every customer

Both rules are part of the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset and the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset (Ruleset ID efb7b8c949ac4650a09736fc376e9aee), with Block as the default action.

Rule description

Rule ID

Ruleset

Default action

Ruby - Heap Overflow - CVE:CVE-2026-132825

7328f23691e44b07892ebd25b19210f1

Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset (Free plan)

Block

Ruby - Heap Overflow - CVE:CVE-2026-132825

1afa543a1ed84893b01df04c34402c88

Cloudflare Managed Ruleset (Pro, Business and Enterprise plans)

Block

Ruby - Integer Overflow - GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px

8660e37e86444f9f9267ba22e9855f05

Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset (Free plan)

Block

Ruby - Integer Overflow - GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px

6defac6a52334542adf4a162daf25922

Cloudflare Managed Ruleset (Pro, Business and Enterprise plans)

Block

On the Free plan, the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset runs automatically, so there is nothing to turn on. On paid plans, the rules are active wherever the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset is deployed. Because paid plans give you more control over how rulesets are deployed, the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset may not be active on every zone. We recommend checking its status to confirm that it is running. You can use the links in the Zero Wire briefing to go straight to the rules in your dashboard.

What the WAF cannot see

A WAF can block an exploit when the malicious input arrives in an HTTP request that passes through Cloudflare. It cannot block every path to the vulnerable code:

  • Traffic that bypasses Cloudflare. Requests sent directly to your origin IP address, and traffic between internal services, never reach the WAF. Configure your origin to accept traffic only from Cloudflare, for example with Cloudflare Tunnel or Authenticated Origin Pulls.
  • Other entry points into the same code. Ruby code that changes the case of strings from email, file imports, message queues or background jobs can reach ruby2shell without an HTTP request.

Adding defense in depth with WAF attack score

Memory corruption is usually only the first step. To run commands, an attacker still has to deliver a second-stage payload, such as shell commands or a reverse shell, and then interact with the compromised server. WAF attack score uses machine learning to score each request for remote code execution payloads, which helps catch exploit variations and post-exploitation traffic that signature-based rules can miss. Create a custom rule that blocks or challenges requests with 

cf.waf.score.rce le 20
 on Enterprise plans, or 
cf.waf.score.class eq "attack"
 on Business plans.

Impact on Cloudflare infrastructure

Cloudflare has patched its systems that use Ruby against ruby2shell. We have found no indication of compromise and continue to monitor.

Patch now

ruby2shell turns a one-byte miscalculation in string case conversion into a pre-authentication path to code execution in default Rails and Sinatra apps. With a public proof of concept expected within days, the window to patch is short. Here is what to do:

  1. Check your WAF coverage. On the Free plan, the ruby2shell rules are already blocking. On paid plans, confirm the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset is deployed and the rules have not been overridden.
  2. Upgrade Ruby to 3.3.14, 3.4.13 or 4.0.10 and restart every Ruby process, including background workers. Rebuild container images. Move applications on Ruby 3.2 or earlier to a supported series.
  3. Update self-hosted products that bundle Ruby, such as GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server, Mastodon, OpenProject and Chatwoot, as each vendor releases a fix. Rebuild Discourse Docker installs now.
  4. Inventory your runtimes. The Zero Wire briefing includes a prompt you can give an AI agent to find every affected Ruby runtime in your infrastructure.

Our WAF analysts will keep updating protections as new techniques appear. Follow the WAF changelog for rule updates.

entries.title: How Cloudflare WAF helps protect against phpAfterShell and other critical PHP flaws
entries.summary: phpAfterShell is a critical flaw in PHP's default session handler that can lead to code execution. Cloudflare WAF blocks it for all customers, including Free plans, and adds new rules for other PHP flaws fixed in the same release.
entries.content:
On November 19, 2026, the security research company depthfirst disclosed phpAfterShell (CVE-2026-126714), a vulnerability in PHP's default file-based session handler that can lead to remote code execution. Under the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) 4.0, it scores 9.2 out of 10 (Critical). The PHP project fixed it the same day in versions 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, and 8.6.0. These releases fix 16 other security vulnerabilities, six of them also rated critical.

Cloudflare’s web application firewall (WAF) blocks known phpAfterShell attack patterns, including for customers on the Free plan. The protection comes from a PHP remote code execution rule we first deployed in October 2026 for the php2shell vulnerabilities. That rule already detected part of the phpAfterShell attack pattern before the vulnerability was disclosed, and on November 19 we updated its detection logic to cover phpAfterShell. The rule is part of both the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset and the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset, is enabled by default, and its default action is Block.

In the same WAF release, we added three new rules to the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset for paid plans: one for a request smuggling flaw in PHP-FPM (CVE-2026-129289), and two for flaws in PHP's SOAP extension (CVE-2026-15353 and CVE-2026-129506) that PHP fixed in the same releases. These rules are enabled by default with the Log action, because the request patterns they look for can also appear in legitimate traffic, and blocking by default could disrupt it. Customers can review matching requests in Security Events now and change the action to Block once they confirm the rules do not affect legitimate traffic.

The WAF is an additional layer of defense, not a replacement for the patch. Several of the critical flaws depend on server configuration or can be reached through paths a WAF does not see, and the only complete fix is to upgrade PHP and restart every worker. Our analysts continue to monitor attack activity and will update the rules as new techniques and variations appear. You can track rule changes in the WAF changelog and follow how the vulnerabilities develop in the dedicated Cloudflare Zero Wire briefing.

There appears to be no indication so far that these vulnerabilities have been exploited. As of November 19, 2026, none of the 17 vulnerabilities was listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and no source we reviewed reports exploitation in the wild.

What we know about phpAfterShell

PHP stores session data in files by default. When an application calls session_start(), PHP reads the session file and deserializes its content into the $_SESSION array. When the request ends, PHP writes the updated session back to the same file.

phpAfterShell is triggered when that write is interrupted. The session file can then hold the beginning of the new session data followed by the end of the old one. On the next request, session_start() deserializes this mixed content. If an attacker controlled the old data, PHP can end up deserializing objects of the attacker's choice.

An attacker trying to exploit the flaw is likely to first search for a way to place controlled data in the session. PHP's advisory names two:

  • Session upload progress, a PHP feature that writes information about a running file upload into the session. A remote client can use it to shape the stored data.
  • Applications that store large user-controlled strings in the session.

According to PHP, code execution also requires an interruption at a useful point in the write and a suitable deserialization gadget chain in the application. depthfirst reports that it reached code execution without an application gadget by chaining a second, undisclosed memory-corruption bug in a PHP-native class. The sources we reviewed do not establish whether that second bug is fixed in the November 19 releases.

depthfirst says it discovered and reported phpAfterShell. The CVE record credits Leo Lin and Asahi as reporters.

Who is affected

The vulnerable versions are PHP 8.2 before 8.2.36, 8.3 before 8.3.37, 8.4 before 8.4.28, 8.5 before 8.5.13, and the 8.6.0 release candidates. Whether a deployment is exposed depends on the conditions of each flaw.

PHP 8.1 and earlier are end-of-life. depthfirst says the official 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1 end-of-life mitigation branches are not affected by phpAfterShell, but PHP says CVE-2026-129289 was introduced in PHP 5.6.0 and that releases older than 8.2 may also be affected by CVE-2026-115560.

Linux distributions often backport fixes without changing the PHP version number. Check the full package version against your distribution's advisory.

How Cloudflare WAF protects you

PHP runs a large share of the web, often inside content management systems, plugins, and container images that teams do not update directly. Patching every PHP runtime takes time. Cloudflare WAF reduces your exposure while you patch.

phpAfterShell: protection on every plan

We released the original PHP remote code execution rules in an emergency release on October 21, 2026, after the php2shell vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) were disclosed. We extended them to CVE-2026-115560 on October 23 and refined them several times in the following weeks, based in part on reports from security researchers who took part in a PHP Capture the Flag (CTF) challenge.

phpAfterShell shares an attack technique with php2shell: an attacker plants serialized PHP data in session storage and waits for PHP to deserialize it. Because of that overlap, the existing rule already matched part of the phpAfterShell attack pattern before disclosure. On November 19, we updated the rule's detection logic to cover phpAfterShell and added CVE-2026-126714 to its description.

What the WAF cannot see

A WAF can block an exploit when the malicious data arrives in an HTTP request that passes through Cloudflare. It cannot block every path to these vulnerabilities, including:

  • The deserialization step. phpAfterShell's final step happens inside PHP, when it reads a corrupted session file. The WAF can block the requests that plant the payload, not the read itself.
  • Session data from other sources. If an application copies user-controlled data into the session from a database, a queue or an upstream API, that data may never cross the WAF in a recognizable form.
  • Flaws triggered by server state. CVE-2026-129496, CVE-2026-129481, CVE-2026-129474 and CVE-2026-129182 depend on error logs, diagnostics and worker lifecycle. They do not have dedicated WAF rules, and the patch and the configuration changes below are the way to address them.
  • Traffic that bypasses Cloudflare. This includes internal traffic between services and PHP-FPM listeners exposed directly to a network.

Adding defense in depth with WAF attack score

WAF attack score adds a machine learning layer that scores each request for attack payloads. It is available on Business plans (cf.waf.score.class) and, with a dedicated remote code execution sub-score (cf.waf.score.rce) along with an overall score (cf.waf.score), on Enterprise plans.

Attack score complements the managed rules. It will not recognize every serialized object or smuggled FastCGI record on its own, but a working exploit chain usually needs more than one request, and the later stages carry payloads the model is trained to score:

  • Second-stage payloads. Once an attacker can run code, they still need to send commands: shell execution primitives (/bin/sh -c, system(), passthru()), PHP code evaluation (eval(), assert()) or reverse-shell strings in headers, query parameters or request bodies.
  • Webshell traffic. Attackers often drop a small PHP webshell after the initial compromise. Requests that pass operating system commands to that webshell remain visible to attack score.

Deploy protections and patch

You can find more information on how to deploy managed rules and attack score in our WAF guide. In short:

  1. Check that phpAfterShell protection is active. On the Free plan, no action is needed. On paid plans, make sure the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset is deployed and that the PHP Remote Code Execution Attack #6 rule is set to Block.
  2. Review the new rules and switch them to Block. The CVE-2026-129289, CVE-2026-15353 and CVE-2026-129506 rules are in Log mode by default. Review their matches in Security Events, then change their action to Block.
  3. Layer attack score. Create a custom rule that blocks or challenges requests with a low remote code execution score, for example cf.waf.score.rce le 20 on Enterprise plans, or cf.waf.score.class eq "attack" on Business plans.
  4. Upgrade PHP. Move to 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13 or 8.6.0. Rebuild container images and restart the PHP-FPM master or Apache so every worker loads the new binary, then verify the version that serves web requests. After upgrading, check that no php.ini, FPM pool or virtual host still sets session.upload_progress.enabled=1, because an explicit setting overrides the new default.
  5. Apply interim mitigations if you cannot upgrade right away. Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and limit the untrusted data you store in sessions. Turn off FastCGI connection reuse. On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces=0. Fix configuration errors that produce PHP startup warnings, or send PHP errors to syslog instead of a file. Keep PHP-FPM listeners off untrusted networks. These steps reduce exposure; they do not fix the flaws.

Update every PHP runtime now

phpAfterShell turns an interrupted file write in PHP's default session handler into a path to code execution, and it arrived in the same release as six other critical flaws. With technical details now public, we expect exploit attempts to follow. Cloudflare WAF blocks known phpAfterShell attack patterns for every customer, including the Free plan, and paid plans have new rules for the PHP-FPM and SOAP flaws. The fix is still to upgrade PHP and restart the services that use it.
